title: Reading a Tissue One Cell at a Time
endLine: Sort cells by RNA; anchor candidate types with location and function.

scenes.tts: How can you tell apart every cell in a tissue? Averaging a whole tissue hides its mix of cells, and the average shifts whenever that mix shifts. To see the mix, read one cell alone.
scenes.caption: How can you tell apart every cell in a tissue? Averaging a whole tissue hides its mix of cells, and the average shifts whenever that mix shifts. To see the mix, read one cell alone.
scenes.visual: Schematic cross-section of living tissue filling over 60% of the frame height, packed with mixed cell shapes (round, branching, and large) containing gently drifting glowing dots (RNA). The question 'How can you tell cells apart?' appears in the first 4 seconds. Below, a schematic single-bar tissue average rises and falls as the mix of cell shapes changes, even while each cell's own glow stays steady; a bright ring then isolates one cell.
scenes.narration: How can you tell apart every cell in a tissue? Averaging a whole tissue hides its mix of cells, and the average shifts whenever that mix shifts. To see the mix, read one cell alone.

scenes.visual: The same tissue cross-section dims slightly in place with ambient glowing dots still drifting; the title 'Reading a Tissue One Cell at a Time' fades in at high contrast, holds, and fades out.

scenes.tts: Every cell in a tissue carries essentially the same genome. So the genome alone cannot separate neighbouring cells. What differs is which genes each cell actively transcribes into R N A. Single-cell R N A sequencing reads that active pattern cell by cell.
scenes.caption: Every cell in a tissue carries essentially the same genome. So the genome alone cannot separate neighbouring cells. What differs is which genes each cell actively transcribes into RNA. Single-cell RNA sequencing reads that active pattern cell by cell.
scenes.visual: Zoom smoothly into two neighbouring cells inside the same schematic tissue cross-section (no molecular structures). Inside both cells, identical calm bars labelled 'Same genome' glow the same colour; then distinct sets of coloured glowing strands labelled 'Active RNA' stream out of each cell, showing different patterns. One cell's active pattern highlights as a readout.
scenes.narration: Every cell in a tissue carries essentially the same genome. So the genome alone cannot separate neighbouring cells. What differs is which genes each cell actively transcribes into RNA. Single-cell RNA sequencing reads that active pattern cell by cell.

scenes.tts: First, enzymes usually separate the tissue into loose single cells. Each cell's captured R N A is copied into D N A. Every copy from one cell gets that cell's unique barcode, a short tag. With those tags attached, all the D N A is pooled and sequenced together.
scenes.caption: First, enzymes usually separate the tissue into loose single cells. Each cell's captured RNA is copied into DNA. Every copy from one cell gets that cell's unique barcode, a short tag. With those tags attached, all the DNA is pooled and sequenced together.
scenes.visual: In the same carried tissue cross-section, gentle waves dissolve the borders between cells so single cells drift apart (schematic). Inside three visible cells, RNA lines copy into abstract schematic DNA bars (no molecular structures), each stamped with its cell's unique coloured stripe labelled 'Cell barcode'. All tagged bars then merge into one moving sequencing stream.
scenes.narration: First, enzymes usually separate the tissue into loose single cells. Each cell's captured RNA is copied into DNA. Every copy from one cell gets that cell's unique barcode, a short tag. With those tags attached, all the DNA is pooled and sequenced together.

scenes.tts: Next, software sorts the sequenced reads by barcode into a count matrix. Rows are genes, columns are cells, and entries count reads or molecules. Software then groups similar cells into a cluster. Comparing cluster genes to known profiles proposes an identity, called annotation.
scenes.caption: Next, software sorts the sequenced reads by barcode into a count matrix. Rows are genes, columns are cells, and entries count reads or molecules. Software then groups similar cells into a cluster. Comparing cluster genes to known profiles proposes an identity, called annotation.
scenes.visual: The pooled sequencing stream sorts by barcode colour into a glowing schematic grid labelled 'Count matrix', with rows labelled 'Genes' and columns labelled 'Cells'. Columns detach and morph into dots in a schematic cluster plot that pull together into colour-coded 'Clusters'; brief identity tags slide onto each group labelled 'Annotation'.
scenes.narration: Next, software sorts the sequenced reads by barcode into a count matrix. Rows are genes, columns are cells, and entries count reads or molecules. Software then groups similar cells into a cluster. Comparing cluster genes to known profiles proposes an identity, called annotation.

scenes.tts: Look closely at those clusters. Software grouped the sampled cells by their R N A into separate groups. Predict: if a cluster has its own gene pattern, is it already a proven cell type?
scenes.caption: Look closely at those clusters. Software grouped the sampled cells by their RNA into separate groups. Predict: if a cluster has its own gene pattern, is it already a proven cell type?
scenes.visual: The schematic cluster plot settles in the centre while the faint ghost outline of the original tissue cross-section appears behind it. One bright cluster pulses as the high-contrast question 'Is every cluster a proven cell type?' fades in above.
scenes.narration: Look closely at those clusters. Software grouped the sampled cells by their RNA into separate groups. Predict: if a cluster has its own gene pattern, is it already a proven cell type?

scenes.visual: Thinking pause: the question 'Is every cluster a proven cell type?' stays on screen. The highlighted schematic cluster slowly stretches as if about to split in two, then drifts gently back, with the faint tissue outline behind it.

scenes.tts: No: treat a cluster as a candidate type, not a measured function. Finer settings or deeper sequencing can split one cluster into two. Cells can enter and leave temporary states, so a cluster may be a state, not a type. Separating tissue also erases locations and probably depletes large, fragile neurons.
scenes.caption: No: treat a cluster as a candidate type, not a measured function. Finer settings or deeper sequencing can split one cluster into two. Cells can enter and leave temporary states, so a cluster may be a state, not a type. Separating tissue also erases locations and probably depletes large, fragile neurons.
scenes.visual: In the schematic cluster plot, a 'Resolution' slider moves right and splits one cluster into two. One cell dot changes colour and returns to show a temporary 'State'. Then the faded tissue cross-section brightens as large fragile neurons break apart during dissociation (schematic) and blank position markers appear where locations were lost.
scenes.narration: No: treat a cluster as a candidate type, not a measured function. Finer settings or deeper sequencing can split one cluster into two. Cells can enter and leave temporary states, so a cluster may be a state, not a type. Separating tissue also erases locations and probably depletes large, fragile neurons.

scenes.tts: Experimenters guard against those traps three ways. Quality control drops cells that fail checks. Spatial transcriptomics, like Merfish or Slide-seek, reads R N A at known tissue positions. A candidate cluster earns a type claim when it recurs and location, shape, or response anchors it.
scenes.caption: Experimenters guard against those traps three ways. Quality control drops cells that fail checks. Spatial transcriptomics, like MERFISH or Slide-seq, reads RNA at known tissue positions. A candidate cluster earns a type claim when it recurs and location, shape, or response anchors it.
scenes.visual: Three safeguards animate on the same carried world (schematic). First, dim ragged dots fade out under 'Quality control'. Second, cluster colours flow from the plot back into fixed grid coordinates inside the intact tissue cross-section under 'Spatial map'. Third, a glowing anchor links one mapped cluster to its tissue position, cell shape, and a schematic electrical response trace.
scenes.narration: Experimenters guard against those traps three ways. Quality control drops cells that fail checks. Spatial transcriptomics, like MERFISH or Slide-seq, reads RNA at known tissue positions. A candidate cluster earns a type claim when it recurs and location, shape, or response anchors it.

scenes.tts: Reading single cells unlocked biology tissue averages hide. In 2015, Hanchate and colleagues sequenced single mouse olfactory neurons. Many immature neurons expressed several receptor genes at low levels, while most mature ones carried one abundant receptor transcript.
scenes.caption: Reading single cells unlocked biology tissue averages hide. In 2015, Hanchate and colleagues sequenced single mouse olfactory neurons. Many immature neurons expressed several receptor genes at low levels, while most mature ones carried one abundant receptor transcript.
scenes.visual: The carried tissue cross-section morphs into a schematic strip of mouse olfactory neurons labelled 'Hanchate et al., 2015'. On the left, immature cells glow dimly with several mixed colours (low-level receptor genes); moving smoothly rightward as cells mature, each mature neuron locks onto one bright single colour (one abundant receptor).
scenes.narration: Reading single cells unlocked biology tissue averages hide. In 2015, Hanchate and colleagues sequenced single mouse olfactory neurons. Many immature neurons expressed several receptor genes at low levels, while most mature ones carried one abundant receptor transcript.

scenes.tts: In 2022, Kamath and colleagues sequenced single nuclei from postmortem human substantia nigra, a midbrain nucleus. They sorted dopamine neurons into ten populations and mapped them with Slide-seek in macaque midbrain. One, marked by A G T R one, was highly susceptible to loss in Parkinson disease.
scenes.caption: In 2022, Kamath and colleagues sequenced single nuclei from postmortem human substantia nigra, a midbrain nucleus. They sorted dopamine neurons into ten populations and mapped them with Slide-seq in macaque midbrain. One, marked by AGTR1, was highly susceptible to loss in Parkinson disease.
scenes.visual: The tissue cross-section transitions smoothly into a schematic midbrain section labelled 'Substantia nigra' and 'Kamath et al., 2022'. Ten colour-coded dopamine neuron populations map onto positions across the section (Slide-seq schematic); nine stay luminous while the one population labelled 'AGTR1' dims sharply to show high susceptibility to loss in Parkinson disease.
scenes.narration: In 2022, Kamath and colleagues sequenced single nuclei from postmortem human substantia nigra, a midbrain nucleus. They sorted dopamine neurons into ten populations and mapped them with Slide-seq in macaque midbrain. One, marked by AGTR1, was highly susceptible to loss in Parkinson disease.

scenes.tts: In 2023, Yao, Zeng and colleagues profiled around seven million adult mouse brain cells. Roughly four million passed quality control and formed five thousand three hundred twenty-two clusters. Merfish, in about four point three million cells from one mouse brain, placed them back in the anatomy. Still, not every cluster may be a true type.
scenes.caption: In 2023, Yao, Zeng and colleagues profiled around seven million adult mouse brain cells. Roughly four million passed quality control and formed 5,322 clusters. MERFISH, in about 4.3 million cells from one mouse brain, placed them back in the anatomy. Still, not every cluster may be a true type.
scenes.visual: Zoom out smoothly from the midbrain slice to a full schematic adult mouse brain cross-section labelled 'Yao, Zeng et al., 2023'. A counter steps from 'Around seven million profiled' to 'Roughly four million passed QC' and '5,322 clusters'; then a sweeping MERFISH scan across 'About 4.3 million cells' paints the cluster colours back into matching anatomical regions, glowing steadily; a small caution note reads 'Not every cluster may be a true type'.

MERFISH, in about 4.3 million cells from one mouse brain, placed them back in the anatomy. Still, not every cluster may be a true type.

scenes.visual: The mapped brain cross-section dims softly to a quiet backdrop as the end-card line appears centred in high contrast: 'Sort cells by RNA; anchor candidate types with location and function.'
